Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded by $y=2{x}^{2}-2$ and $y=1-{x}^{2},$ shown above?

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the intersection points between the two graphs occur when $x=-1$ and $x=1.$ So these will be our limits of integration.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/c6390f35fb796517054a15f16ee12f1354fa04f315f3cf1d91d498f19e73e15b.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=2{x}^{2}-2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=1-{x}^{2}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[\,(1-{x}^{2})-(2{x}^{2}-2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-3{x}^{2}+3)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded between $g(x)=2-{x}^{2}-2x$ and $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+6x-1,$ shown above?

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2-{x}^{2}-2x & =2{x}^{2}+6x-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}+8x-3 & =0 \\ x & =\frac{-8\pm \sqrt{{8}^{2}-4\cdot 3\cdot (-3)}}{2\cdot 3} \\  & =\frac{-8\pm 10}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-3$ to $x=\frac{1}{3}.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/abfea1f4299a0e8ca980e817fda49f0d125cc11cbaae7dae85e5deca7d513c9f.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=2{x}^{2}+6x-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=2-{x}^{2}-2x.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-3}^{1/3}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1/3}[\,(2-{x}^{2}-2x)-(2{x}^{2}+6x-1)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{1/3}(-3{x}^{2}-8x+3)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded between $y={x}^{2}-4x+3$ and $y=x-1?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/c286710c66df6613cf448089a76902e63ed4783d31a89c728d5022a382ce3ddf.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+3 & =x-1 \\ {x}^{2}-5x+4 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=1$ to $x=4.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/af15b99ba9e1233c76b6089fb1b4fb6cb62b9edcbedc7f0a241212075be3d33c.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{2}-4x+3,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=x-1.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{1}^{4}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}[\,(x-1)-({x}^{2}-4x+3)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(-{x}^{2}+5x-4)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ of the finite region enclosed between $y=-3{x}^{2}+8$ and $y=-{x}^{2},$ shown above. Do not round the answer.

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

$A=$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{x}^{2}+8 & =-{x}^{2} \\ -2{x}^{2}+8 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-2$ to $x=2.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/336a1503663239debacda06ca200e47151493ffbc94c3b797afb274c3355db97.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=-{x}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=-3{x}^{2}+8.$

We can now set up the integration with our $x$ values (Top-Bottom):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[(-3{x}^{2}+8)-(-{x}^{2})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(-2{x}^{2}+8)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(8-2{x}^{2})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the integrand is an even function. Therefore, we can find the area as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}(8-2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{(8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2((8\cdot 2-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {2}^{3})-0) \\  & =2((16-\frac{16}{3})-(0)) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{32}{3} \\  & =\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the area of the finite region bounded by the curves $y=-{x}^{2}-2$ and $y=-x-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/af2b16006d5616854a3fb4e5f116c84375ee78f633ab8f313045b3d6feed922b.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-2 & =-x-2 \\ x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(1-x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/bf320ce6791c3f776961fee7fe3b7714895a3f5e38d8d721fd653ee816eb8997.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=-x-2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=-{x}^{2}-2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(-{x}^{2}-2)-(-x-2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3})-(0-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the area of the finite region enclosed between $f(x) =x^2-2x+2$ and $g(x) = 2,$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/01f139c53b6328341b463f5ad941d37fccb241fff109c0584207017341e8e5f7.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+2 & =2 \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/39798ef4ff6e898527864628dc2750f88b115c03b2d6b8fb729f30b21d2d2bf5.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=x^2-2x+2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=2.$

Therefore, we can find the area as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(2)-({x}^{2}-2x+2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-{x}^{2}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =({2}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{3})-(0-0) \\  & =(4-\frac{8}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we want to find the finite area bounded between the curves $y=x^2$ and $y=1.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/af462c91b8348f2daf5c38a7e705bad3b055919269114e80608a5aa0536a7b01.png)

The area $A$ of the region is given by

$$
A = \int_{-1}^{1} \left[\, \left(\color{brown}{\textrm{upper function}}\right) - \left(\color{blue}{\textrm{lower function}}\right) \,\right] \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

So in our case, the area is expressed as

$$
A = \int_{-1}^{1} \big[ ({\color{brown}{1}}) - ({\color{blue}{x^2}}) \big]\,\textrm{d}x = \int_{-1}^{1} (1-x^2)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Now that the integral has been written down correctly, we can evaluate it using the usual techniques:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =[1-\frac{1}{3}]-[-1-\frac{(-1)^{3}}{3}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-[-\frac{2}{3}] \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So the area of the region is $\dfrac{4}{3}.$

Lastly, let's recap a few things:

- The limits of integration correspond to the $x$-values at the points of intersection of the two functions.

- If you're not sure which is the lower function and which is the upper, one way to find out is to draw a vertical line that *points upward* through the region, like so:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/00a80b851fbb08d25a110c8532606830271744e9ccb1377a43949def5af9f308.png)

The vertical line always 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=x^2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=1.$

tutorials.content:
Suppose that we want to find the finite area bounded between the curves $y=x^2$ and $y=1.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/af462c91b8348f2daf5c38a7e705bad3b055919269114e80608a5aa0536a7b01.png)

The area $A$ of the region is given by

$$
A = \int_{-1}^{1} \left[\, \left(\color{brown}{\textrm{upper function}}\right) - \left(\color{blue}{\textrm{lower function}}\right) \,\right] \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

So in our case, the area is expressed as

$$
A = \int_{-1}^{1} \big[ ({\color{brown}{1}}) - ({\color{blue}{x^2}}) \big]\,\textrm{d}x = \int_{-1}^{1} (1-x^2)\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

Now that the integral has been written down correctly, we can evaluate it using the usual techniques:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =[1-\frac{1}{3}]-[-1-\frac{(-1)^{3}}{3}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-[-\frac{2}{3}] \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So the area of the region is $\dfrac{4}{3}.$

Lastly, let's recap a few things:

- The limits of integration correspond to the $x$-values at the points of intersection of the two functions.

- If you're not sure which is the lower function and which is the upper, one way to find out is to draw a vertical line that *points upward* through the region, like so:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/00a80b851fbb08d25a110c8532606830271744e9ccb1377a43949def5af9f308.png)

The vertical line always 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=x^2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=1.$

tutorials.name: Justifying the Rule
tutorials.problem:
Lastly, let's discuss why the area formula works.

$$
A = \int_{a}^{b}\left(\color{brown}{\textrm{upper function}}\right) - \left(\color{blue}{\textrm{lower function}}\right)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

Consider the area bounded by the two functions $y = f(x)$ and $y = g(x).$ We'll assume that the two curves intersect at $x=\pm 1,$ and for $x\in(-1,1)$ we have $f(x) > g(x),$ so $f(x)$ is the upper function.

We can approximate the area using rectangles in the following way. First, we will divide the interval $[-1,1]$ into small subintervals of equal length $\Delta{x}.$ One such subinterval is shown in the picture below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/4c8c171e7b57a566fe7372248ad6e77d6a756e91cfc1a164a0d60fa042a38462.png)

The area $\Delta{A}$ bounded between the curves $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ can be approximated by the area of the rectangle shown below, with the sides $\Delta{x}$ (horizontal) and $f(x)-g(x)$ (vertical),

$$
\Delta{A} \approx \left(f(x)-g(x)\right)\Delta{x}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/209ddeac16dc7a83b49f871adfaf81ef78296009ea2fb0ffc8e7d2d4554e0a55.png)

The sum over all the rectangles will approximate the total area $A$ that we want. This approximation becomes more accurate as the rectangles get narrower, i.e., $\Delta{x} \to 0.$ And the limit of the sum, as $\Delta x \to 0,$ is the required integral!

$$
\begin{aligned}A={\int }_{a}^{b}(f(x)-g(x))\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$
tutorials.title: Justifying the Rule
tutorials.content:
Lastly, let's discuss why the area formula works.

$$
A = \int_{a}^{b}\left(\color{brown}{\textrm{upper function}}\right) - \left(\color{blue}{\textrm{lower function}}\right)\,\textrm{d}x
$$

Consider the area bounded by the two functions $y = f(x)$ and $y = g(x).$ We'll assume that the two curves intersect at $x=\pm 1,$ and for $x\in(-1,1)$ we have $f(x) > g(x),$ so $f(x)$ is the upper function.

We can approximate the area using rectangles in the following way. First, we will divide the interval $[-1,1]$ into small subintervals of equal length $\Delta{x}.$ One such subinterval is shown in the picture below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/4c8c171e7b57a566fe7372248ad6e77d6a756e91cfc1a164a0d60fa042a38462.png)

The area $\Delta{A}$ bounded between the curves $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ can be approximated by the area of the rectangle shown below, with the sides $\Delta{x}$ (horizontal) and $f(x)-g(x)$ (vertical),

$$
\Delta{A} \approx \left(f(x)-g(x)\right)\Delta{x}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/209ddeac16dc7a83b49f871adfaf81ef78296009ea2fb0ffc8e7d2d4554e0a55.png)

The sum over all the rectangles will approximate the total area $A$ that we want. This approximation becomes more accurate as the rectangles get narrower, i.e., $\Delta{x} \to 0.$ And the limit of the sum, as $\Delta x \to 0,$ is the required integral!

$$
\begin{aligned}A={\int }_{a}^{b}(f(x)-g(x))\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$
